Question: One fair die has faces \(1,\) \(1,\) \(2,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(3\) and another has faces \(4,\) \(4,\) \(5,\) \(5,\) \(6,\) \(6.\) The dice are rolled and the numbers on the top faces are added. What is the probability that the sum will be odd?
Solution:
A sum is odd exactly when one number is odd and the other is even. Treat the six physical faces of each die as distinct, even when their numbers agree. The two rolls give \(6\cdot6=36\) equally likely face pairs.

The first die has \(4\) odd faces and \(2\) even faces. The second has \(4\) even faces and \(2\) odd faces. Thus there are \(4\cdot4=16\) pairs with an odd first number and an even second number, and \(2\cdot2=4\) pairs with an even first number and an odd second number. These cases are disjoint and include every odd sum.

The probability is therefore
\[
\frac{16+4}{36}=\boxed{\frac59},
\]
choice D.
